summary: Defines a MIB module for managing networks that use the Precision Time Protocol from IEEE 1588-2008. It is written to be compliant with SMIv2 and semantically identical to the SMIv1 definitions.

eli5.summary: A dashboard to check and manage clocks that keep very exact time across a network.

subtitle: A read-only SNMP MIB that lets operators monitor Precision Time Protocol clocks across a network.

tldr.problem: Operators had no standard SNMP way to look at the state of IEEE 1588-2008 Precision Time Protocol clocks, which are often embedded in routers, switches and gateways.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8173 defines the PTPBASE-MIB module, with tables that expose read-only PTP data sets for ordinary, boundary and transparent clocks and their ports.
tldr.outcome: Operators can monitor PTP clock operation through SNMP. The module is read-only, so configuring clocks stays with each device's own interface.

today: RFC 8173 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2017. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 8173 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for managing devices that run the Precision Time Protocol (PTP) from IEEE Std. 1588-2008. It covers PTP ordinary clocks, transparent clocks and boundary clocks.

The module is restricted to reading standard PTP data elements, so it monitors how PTP clocks operate. It is intended for the default PTP profile running over IP. The authors expect other managed objects to be defined later to measure clock performance for profiles such as the Telecom Profile in ITU-T G.8265.1, and say that is out of scope. Some other profiles have their own MIB modules, and this one is not meant to replace them.

It is also read-only. Since PTP clocks are often embedded in other network elements, configuration is generally done through the element's own configuration interface.
sections.eli5: It is a window onto clocks, not a set of knobs. You can see what time each clock thinks it is, but you change settings somewhere else.

sections.title: SNMP and the SMIv2 Setting
sections.content:
Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store called the MIB, generally using the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). Objects are described with the Structure of Management Information. This module is written to be compliant with SMIv2, the version described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580, and the abstract adds that it is semantically identical to the peer SMIv1 definitions. The overall framework is outlined in RFC 3410.

The RFC does not re-explain PTP. It points to Section 6 of IEEE 1588-2008 for an overview of synchronization networks and to Section 3.1 for the meaning of terms. The module description says PTP lets clocks of various precision, resolution and stability synchronize to a grandmaster clock, and that this module addresses PTPv2, not PTPv1.
sections.eli5: SNMP is the language network gadgets use to answer questions about themselves. This document adds the clock questions to that language.

sections.title: Textual Conventions
sections.content:
The module first defines a set of textual conventions, which are named data types that give PTP concepts a consistent form in SNMP. Examples include:

  • PtpClockDomainType: a domain number from 0 to 255 that groups PTP devices.
  • PtpClockIdentity: an 8-octet clock identity, normally taken from IEEE EUI-64 assignments.
  • PtpClockType: ordinaryClock (1), boundaryClock (2), transparentClock (3) or boundaryNode (4).
  • PtpClockPortState: the protocol engine state of a port, from initializing (1) to slave (9).
  • PtpClockMechanismType: end-to-end (1), peer-to-peer (2) or disabled (254) delay measurement.
  • PtpClockProfileType: default (1), telecom (2) or vendor specific (3).
  • PtpClockStateType: freerun, holdover, acquiring, frequencyLocked or phaseAligned.

Others describe clock quality class and accuracy, and the time source, which is enumerated from atomic clock (16) and GPS (32) through PTP (64) and NTP (80) to internal oscillator (160). Each convention points to the section of IEEE 1588-2008 it mirrors.
sections.eli5: Before listing the questions, the document agrees on names for the answers, like "master" or "slave", so every device writes them the same way.

sections.title: Tables of Clock Information
sections.content:
The module is registered as ptpbaseMIB at { mib-2 241 }. It has three parts: notifications, objects and conformance. The objects are split into system information and clock information.

It defines 13 tables. The system tables give counts of clock ports per domain and of domains per clock type, plus a scalar for the PTP profile in use. The clock tables mirror the IEEE 1588 data sets: currentDS (steps removed, offset from master, mean path delay), parentDS (the parent and grandmaster clock identity, priorities and quality), defaultDS, running state, timePropertiesDS (UTC offset, leap seconds, traceability and time source) and the transparent clock default data set.

Port tables describe each clock port: its general information, portDS intervals and delay mechanism, running state, packet counters, transparent clock port data and the peer ports associated with it. Clock entries are indexed by domain number, clock type and instance, so one device can report several clocks.
sections.eli5: Imagine a big chart with one row per clock and per port. Each column is a fact, such as how far this clock is from the boss clock.

sections.title: Compliance and Object Groups
sections.content:
The end of the module defines four compliance statements, covering system information, clock information, clock port information and transparent clock information. These tell implementers which parts they must support depending on the kind of PTP device they offer.

Twelve object groups collect the objects: system info, the current, parent, default, running, time properties and transparent data sets, and the port, port data set, port running, port transparent data set and port associate groups. A device claims compliance by implementing the groups that fit the clock types it runs.
sections.eli5: It is a checklist. A device says which clock jobs it does, and the checklist says which answers it must be able to give.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No object in this module has a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create. If it is implemented correctly, an intruder cannot alter or create the objects with SNMP SET operations.

The readable objects can still be sensitive in some networks, because they expose clock status, data sets and port information. The RFC therefore says to control even GET and NOTIFY access and possibly to encrypt the values on the wire. SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and deploying them is NOT recommended. Implementations SHOULD provide the SNMPv3 security features, and those claiming compliance with SNMPv3 MUST support authentication and privacy through the User-based Security Model with AES. It is the operator's responsibility to give access only to legitimate users.
sections.eli5: Even a window can show private things. So only people with the right key should be allowed to look through it.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The only IANA action is the object identifier for the module. IANA recorded ptpbaseMIB as { mib-2 241 } in the Structure of Management Information Numbers (MIB Module Registrations) registry.
sections.eli5: The module got its own official address number so nobody else uses the same one.
